entries.title: Trump Signals Further Interest in Working With Democrats on ‘TrumpCare’
entries.summary: The president reposted a photo of Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s message promoting health care for “every American, from cradle to grave.”
entries.content:
President Donald Trump reposted incoming Michigan Senator Abdul El-Sayed’s mockups of a plan for “TrumpCare” gold cards on Saturday — the latest indication the president may be willing to work with the incoming Democratic majority on health care proposals.

El-Sayed, a Democrat whose midterms campaign centered on passing Medicare for All, uploaded on Nov. 12 pictures of a golden insurance card emblazoned with the word “TrumpCare” in a post directed to the president.

“Donald, this is on the table. Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave,” El-Sayed wrote.

Trump’s repost on Truth Social Saturday included no commentary.

Earlier Saturday, Trump told Fox News that Democrats “have some good points on health care.”

“There’s a chance we could get great health care, and a lot of other things, and we do it in a bipartisan way,” the president said. “There’s a very good chance — because otherwise, everything gets vetoed.”

On Friday, the president said Democrats had called him to discuss health care and immigration reform, similarly indicating he would work with the soon-to-be majority party, though he did not indicate with whom he had spoken.

El-Sayed’s Nov. 12 post was followed by a video the next week in which he called for passing “Trumpcare for All.”

“You want to be the most popular president in the history of America,” he said in the video, gesturing to a framed illustration of Trump as Jesus and a picture of the golden insurance card. “It’s really popular, people really want health care. You can put your name all over it. You can even give them a gold card.”

On Saturday, El-Sayed reiterated his openness to working with Trump and other Democratic senators to pass guaranteed health care.

“If the President is serious about meeting the unmet promise of guaranteed healthcare in this country, I’m ready to work alongside leaders in the Senate like Senators Van Hollen, Sanders, Wyden, and Warren to deliver,” El-Sayed said in a statement following Trump’s repost.

“President Trump, give me a call. I’m happy to chat," he said.
entries.author: Michelle Del Rey

entries.title: The Spirit Is Denied Its Championship Moment in a 2-1 Loss to the Current
entries.summary: Washington couldn't take advantage of its home field, falling in the NWSL final for a third straight year.
entries.content:
In a chippy, choppy NWSL championship match at Audi Field on Saturday, the Washington Spirit fell to the Kansas City Current, 2-1 — the franchise’s third consecutive loss in the league final.

"This one hurts way worse than any of the other ones," Spirit star Trinity Rodman said after the match. "I don’t even think you have words in this moment — it’s too fresh. But we’re all proud of each other. We’re all gonna be together no matter what."

Playing for a title in front of its home crowd for the first time in franchise history, Washington was forced into a physical game from the very start. Rodman went down early after a collision and briefly left the field, ultimately returning to play after a few minutes, albeit rather gingerly. Both teams struggled to find any sort of offensive rhythm. The clubs set a record for fouls in the first half of a championship game with 19, and they continued apace in the second.

“I don’t think that physicality is something new for them,” midfielder Andi Sullivan said of the Current. “It’s a very fine line of returning the favor.”

Kansas City's first goal came early in the second half on a corner kick from Vanessa DiBernardo. It was the second consecutive playoff game where the Spirit conceded an “Olimpico,” a goal straight off a corner kick, with no other players making contact with the ball. The Spirit had the possession advantage for much of the rest of the second half and created several big chances. Coach Adrián González pushed every button that he could with his substitution options, but nothing came through for the Spirit.

Most of the evening's drama came during a long and hectic period of stoppage time. Kansas City went up 2-0 on a counterattack that looked to be the dagger. But Washington responded shortly after, as Rodman headed in a goal that reignited the home crowd. In one final push, Washington launched a furious series of attacks until the final whistle. None prevailed.

"It obviously sucks to lose, but you got to give credit to Kansas," Rodman said. "They were very dominant, they were very together and they finished their chances. So you can’t be mad.”

The energy of a sold-out crowd was felt throughout the match, as the volume picked up at any scoring chance and boos rained down upon the referees late. Outside the stadium, the vibe was high as locals reflected on the journey that had led to this night.

“We used to play at a high school soccerplex in Maryland, now we sell out a 19,000-seat stadium, like, every week,” said Alison Cassady, a D.C. resident of 25 years and season ticket holder. “I love seeing it.”

Cassady was one of the many fans who walked to the game from The Wharf on Saturday afternoon. They marched alongside a live band that blared hits like “September” and “Livin' on a Prayer,” and led the crowd in chants.

They danced down Southwest D.C. streets, twirling flags and waving foam glowsticks that burned blue against the night sky. Many came with their young children — one determined mother even pushed her infant in a stroller.

As the hype train pulled up to Audi Field, the stadium was playing Beyoncé’s "Who Run the World (Girls)." This, fans hoped, would be their moment.

But hours later, it was the opponent and its fans who celebrated at the final whistle. Rodman, sitting on the pitch, put her hands to her face to cover a steady stream of tears as Current players formed a joyous huddle.

“It's heartbreaking,” fan Randall Marshall said after the loss. “I feel like, overall, we outplayed them. But sometimes that's the beautiful game, right? That one play, it just is not enough to lift the trophy.”
entries.author: Emma Baccellieri

entries.title: Trump Administration Confirms Plans to Detonate Iowa Lead Without a Permit
entries.summary: The Army said cold temperatures are more dangerous for the explosives now because preparations removed bunker doors that had insulated them.
entries.content:
The Trump administration said it intends to detonate lead explosives in Iowa this week despite a court order temporarily blocking it, pointing to the risk of an uncontrolled explosion in cold weather that makes it too dangerous to wait.

In court filings Saturday, Justice Department attorneys laid out why the Army plans to use emergency authority granted by the Environmental Protection Agency to move forward without a permit, and acting Army Secretary Adam Telle for the first time described in greater detail how the situation became so dangerous.

The 68 barrels of degrading lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant are crystallizing, and the crystals are more likely to break in cold temperatures, setting off an explosive chain reaction that could “cause an uncontrolled dispersal of lead azide into the environment,” the DOJ filing says. Temperatures are forecast to drop below freezing Sunday night and then into the low twenties Monday and Tuesday night.

And the Army said its preparations to detonate the explosives have made the situation even more dangerous and cannot be reversed, since heavy metal blast doors were removed and replaced with temporary plywood insulated with foam.

“The bunkers, where the barrels are located, are now more vulnerable to temperature changes because the blast doors were removed in preparation of the controlled detonation and cannot be replaced,” the DOJ filing says.

The Army has been under intense pressure from Iowa and Illinois leaders and from environmental groups, all urging the Defense Department to delay its plan to deliberately destroy the lead azide in an effort to avoid an uncontrolled explosion from the volatile substance. Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds said she was not notified of the Army’s plan until Monday, when it first published maps that showed the possibility of a toxic lead dust plume stretching over parts of Iowa and into Illinois.

Environmental groups filed a lawsuit Thursday intended to delay the explosion, and on Friday the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals temporarily blocked the EPA’s emergency permit. The detonation is currently scheduled to take place Monday.

The Trump administration’s legal response Saturday confirms that the Army intends to blow up the explosives without a permit even if the court decides to continue blocking it, exercising emergency authority granted by the EPA.

In the event of an uncontrolled detonation, the filing describes the dangerous scenarios envisioned by Army experts. An uncontrolled explosion could send lead into the air over unprepared surrounding communities, causing public panic. Some of the lead azide could be jettisoned into other parts of the ammunition plant, undetonated in the initial reaction, necessitating secondary explosions in areas also unprepared for such work.

“Unfavorable winds could increase the dispersion of lead dust into the community,” the DOJ filing said. “An uncontrolled deportation of nearly five tons of primary explosive would endanger soldiers, contractors, and the surrounding communities, all without many of the protective measures meant to minimize the risks from the blast — harm that cannot be undone.”

Telle, in a court declaration, said the Army found that 58 of the 68 barrels have crystallization present around their lids during a late April inspection, meaning the lids of the barrels aren’t safe to remove. The Army first discovered there was a problem with the barrels in March, during a routine inspection, and then prohibited Army personnel from accessing the barrels at that point onward, according to EPA permitting documents obtained by The Washington Sun.

A contractor — American Ordnance — is usually in charge of opening the barrel lids every September to refill the liquid that historically has covered the lead azide and is used to prevent crystallization. But this year, the contractor has not refilled the liquid because of the safety issues, increasing the risks, Telle said in the declaration.

The Army has been preparing mitigation measures for more than a month, building barriers around the site where the lead azide is stored and planning to soak the area ahead of and after the explosion to limit lead dust dispersion.

The environmental groups challenging the Army’s plan also filed a declaration Sunday from explosives and EPA experts, who said that they believed the Army’s mitigation measures would have significantly reduced the risk of explosion from quickly falling temperatures.

“Based on my training and experience, the storage conditions described in EPA's permit, and historical and forecast weather for the Burlington area, it is my opinion that the forecast weather does not support the Army's position that the detonation must occur no later than November 23, 2026,” wrote Mark J. Thomas, a retired EPA official from Region 7, the area that oversees the ammunition plant.

The Army hired a contractor in April to dispose of the explosives using chemicals but then canceled the contract two months later for safety reasons, according to The New York Times. The contract was worth $30,000 and cancelled on May 27, according to federal government contracting records reviewed by The Sun.

entries.title: U.S. Intelligence Chief Says Trump Calling Putin a ‘Friend’ Is ‘Entirely Appropriate’
entries.summary: Following Trump's historic trilateral meeting last week, the director of national intelligence also faced questions about China’s access to U.S. chips.
entries.content:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton defended President Donald Trump calling Russian President Vladimir Putin “a friend,” with Clayton saying Sunday he “completely” trusts Trump and “whatever language the president wants to use.”

Trump called Putin a “friend” in person last week ahead of their historic trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping. Trump also posted a photo of him shaking hands with Putin, captioned “my friend,” on Truth Social on Saturday.

“In that circle — in that circle of that conversation, using the term ‘friend’ is entirely appropriate,” Clayton said on ABC's “This Week.”

Asked by ABC’s Jonathan Karl specifically about whether Putin is America’s friend, the intelligence director responded that Putin “is not America's friend in Ukraine. Not at all.”

On CNN, Clayton brushed off concerns about Trump using the term of endearment with Putin by celebrating Trump as the “greatest conductor of foreign policy in a very challenging time that we have seen.”

“Getting the three nuclear powers together and getting them to agree that they are not going to escalate, that they are going to communicate, that is historic. That is remarkable,” Clayton said on CNN’s “State of the Union.” “And in that context, whatever language the president wants to use, I trust him completely.”

When asked if personally he sees Putin as a friend to the U.S., Clayton added that “in different contexts, you can use a different word.”

Putin has remained a complex geopolitical figure for Trump, with their at times more cordial relationship standing in stark contrast to longstanding U.S. foreign policy; Russia’s invasion and continued war with Ukraine has drawn scrutiny from both Democratic and Republican lawmakers pushing for stronger U.S. support for Ukraine.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy labelled Putin a “killer” on Saturday, reacting to Trump’s comments on the Russian leader, and also said it was a “mistake” for Trump to meet one-on-one with Putin without involvement of Ukraine officials. Trump has blamed the Ukrainian leader for continuing the war and refusing to make concessions to Russia.

Trump met with both Putin and Xi in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday, but despite talks about the Russia-Ukraine war and the U.S.-Iran war, the leaders did not reach a major nuclear agreement.

As the head of U.S. intelligence operations, Clayton also faced questions about the U.S. relationship with China amid reports that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, a major Trump ally in the computer chip-making industry, carried out an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

“This is a matter under investigation,” Clayton told CNN when asked about Alice Huang, the woman U.S. officials say may be a Chinese intelligence operative. “I’m going to let that investigation play out.”

The U.S. and China are primary competitors in the tech race and the advanced chips can be used to power AI systems and data centers.

Following the summit, Trump said only older chips should be sold to China — upholding U.S. export control policy barring China from accessing the more advanced processing units — but noted that the U.S. and China are working on a “very comprehensive deal.”

The Trump administration closed a loophole last week that allowed countries like China to remotely access the more advanced chips, as the Nvidia fallout prompted questions from lawmakers about whether China had access to the technology.

Asked to reassure Americans that China did not get access to the advanced chips, Clayton said “every country is trying to get a hold of them” so he expects “that there are channels through which China was able to get ahold of them.”

Clayton also referred to a case in which Chinese operatives had been charged by the U.S. for conspiring to share the technology with China, saying it “appears based on the facts alleged in the indictment that there was access to those chips.”

The intelligence director cited the high demand for “exquisite technology” of these chips, telling Fox News Sunday that the U.S. should “lead in the buildout” in this sector.

“We do want U.S. chips — just not the most exquisite ones — to be disseminated around the globe,” Clayton said.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin
